claims.text: Partial immunity is lost quickly; VFR travelers have the same risk as nonimmune travelers; past malaria still needs prevention
claims.quote: The partial immunity acquired through continuous exposure to malaria is lost quickly, and VFR travelers should be considered to have the same risk of malaria as other nonimmune travelers.

claims.text: Sporadic-case destinations: mosquito avoidance only, no pills
claims.quote: CDC recommends that travelers use mosquito avoidance measures only, and no chemoprophylaxis.

claims.text: Risk varies by traveler and region, even within one country
claims.quote: The risk of acquiring malaria differs substantially from traveler to traveler and from region to region, even within a single country.

claims.text: 2019: 93% acquired in Africa; 76% of US civilians visiting friends and relatives
claims.quote: 93% were acquired in Africa, 4% in Asia, 2% in the Caribbean and the Americas, and <1% in Oceania and the Middle East. Of U.S. civilians with malaria who reported a reason for travel, 76% were visiting friends and relatives.

claims.text: Regimens taken before, during and after travel; starting before puts drug in blood before exposure
claims.quote: All recommended malaria chemoprophylaxis regimens involve taking a medicine before, during, and after travel to an area with malaria. Beginning the drug before travel allows the antimalarial agent to be in the blood

claims.text: A-P starts 1-2 days before, daily with food, 7 days after; most common AEs
claims.quote: Chemoprophylaxis should begin 1–2 days before travel to malaria-endemic areas; the medication should then be taken daily, with food, ideally at the same time each day, while in malaria-endemic areas, and daily for 7 days after leaving

claims.text: A-P most common adverse effects
claims.quote: The most common adverse effects reported in people using atovaquone-proguanil for chemoprophylaxis or treatment are abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, and headache.

claims.text: A-P not for pregnancy, breastfeeding infants under 5 kg, severe renal impairment; warfarin
claims.quote: Atovaquone-proguanil is not recommended for chemoprophylaxis in children weighing <5 kg (<11 lb), pregnant women, women breastfeeding infants <5 kg, or patients with severe renal impairment (creatinine clearance <30 mL/min).

claims.text: Proguanil increases warfarin effect; INR monitoring
claims.quote: Proguanil can increase the effect of warfarin, so travelers might need international normalized ratio monitoring or adjustment of warfarin dosage.

claims.text: A-P tends to be more expensive, especially for long trips; well tolerated
claims.quote: Tends to be more expensive than some of the other options, especially for long trips

claims.text: A-P well tolerated, side effects uncommon
claims.quote: Well-tolerated and side effects uncommon

claims.text: Adult A-P dose 1 adult tablet 250/100 daily
claims.quote: Atovaquone 250 mg / proguanil 100 mg 1 adult tablet taken orally, 1×/day

claims.text: Doxycycline 100 mg daily, 1-2 days before, 4 weeks after, at least 1 hour before bedtime
claims.quote: Take at least 1 hour before bedtime; avoid lying down within 30 minutes of taking a dose

claims.text: Doxycycline adult dose 100 mg daily
claims.quote: 100 mg taken orally, 1x/day

claims.text: Doxycycline start and stop
claims.quote: Doxycycline chemoprophylaxis should begin 1–2 days before travel to malaria-endemic areas. Doxycycline should be taken once a day during travel in malaria-endemic areas and daily for 4 weeks after the traveler leaves endemic areas.

claims.text: Minocycline users switch to doxycycline 1-2 days before and restart after
claims.quote: People on a long-term regimen of minocycline who need malaria chemoprophylaxis should stop taking minocycline 1–2 days before travel and start doxycycline instead.

claims.text: Doxycycline photosensitivity and yeast infections
claims.quote: Doxycycline can cause photosensitivity, usually manifested as an exaggerated sunburn reaction.

claims.text: Doxycycline vaginal yeast infections
claims.quote: Doxycycline use is associated with an increased frequency of vaginal yeast infections.

claims.text: Doxycycline GI and esophagitis advice
claims.quote: To reduce the risk for esophagitis, advise travelers to swallow the medicine with sufficient fluids and to avoid taking doxycycline before lying down or going to bed.

claims.text: Doxycycline with a meal reduces GI effects
claims.quote: Gastrointestinal side effects (e.g., nausea, vomiting) can be minimized by taking the drug with a meal

claims.text: Doxycycline for acne users; other infections
claims.quote: People already taking doxycycline chronically to prevent acne do not have to take an additional medicine

claims.text: Doxycycline prevents other infections
claims.quote: Doxycycline also can prevent other infections (e.g., rickettsial infections, leptospirosis)

claims.text: Doxycycline contraindicated in pregnancy; Ty21a 24 hours before
claims.quote: Vaccination with the oral typhoid vaccine Ty21a should be completed ≥24 hours before taking a dose of doxycycline.

claims.text: Mefloquine dose 228 mg base weekly, start at least 2 weeks before, 4 weeks after
claims.quote: 228 mg base (250 mg salt) taken orally, 1x/week

claims.text: Mefloquine start at least 2 weeks before travel
claims.quote: Begin taking ≥2 weeks before travel to malaria-endemic areas

claims.text: Mefloquine can be started 3-4 weeks ahead
claims.quote: mefloquine can be started 3–4 weeks in advance to allow potential adverse events to be evaluated before travel.

claims.text: Mefloquine side effects and rare serious reactions
claims.quote: Mefloquine has been associated with rare but serious adverse reactions (e.g., psychosis, seizures) when taken at prophylactic doses

claims.text: Mefloquine other side effects
claims.quote: Other side effects reported in chemoprophylaxis studies include abnormal dreams, anxiety disorder, depression, dizziness, gastrointestinal disturbance, headache, insomnia, and visual disturbances.

claims.text: Mefloquine limits: psychiatric conditions, seizures, cardiac conduction, resistance; long trips; pregnancy
claims.quote: Can be used in all trimesters of pregnancy and during breastfeeding

claims.text: Mefloquine not for cardiac conduction abnormalities
claims.quote: Mefloquine is not recommended for people with cardiac conduction abnormalities.

claims.text: Mefloquine contraindications
claims.quote: Mefloquine is contraindicated in people with active depression, a recent history of depression, generalized anxiety disorder, psychosis, schizophrenia and other major psychiatric disorders, or seizures.

claims.text: Mefloquine resistance areas
claims.quote: Cannot be used in areas with mefloquine-resistant Plasmodium spp.

claims.text: Mefloquine FDA medication guide
claims.quote: Any traveler receiving a prescription for mefloquine must also receive a copy of the FDA medication guide.

claims.text: Chloroquine 300 mg base weekly, 1-2 weeks before, 4 weeks after; psoriasis
claims.quote: 300 mg base (500 mg salt) taken orally, 1x/week

claims.text: Chloroquine start 1-2 weeks before; can exacerbate psoriasis
claims.quote: Begin taking 1–2 weeks before travel to malaria-endemic areas Take 1x/week, on the same day each week, while in malaria-endemic areas Continue taking 1x/week for another 4 weeks after leaving endemic areas Can exacerbate psoriasis

claims.text: Chloroquine resistance everywhere except Caribbean and Central America west of Panama Canal
claims.quote: Chloroquine-resistant P. falciparum is found in all parts of the world (Africa, Asia, South America) except the Caribbean and Central American countries west of the Panama Canal.

claims.text: Primaquine dose 30 mg base daily, 1-2 days before, 7 days after
claims.quote: 30 mg base (52.6 mg salt) taken orally, 1x/day

claims.text: Primaquine schedule
claims.quote: primaquine should be taken 1–2 days before travel to malaria-endemic areas, daily, with food, ideally at the same time each day, while in the malaria-endemic area, and daily for 7 days after leaving the area

claims.text: Primaquine for P. vivax areas
claims.quote: One of the most effective drugs for prevention of P. vivax; thus, a good choice for travel to places with >90% P. vivax

claims.text: Primaquine two uses incl. terminal prophylaxis; GI upset with food
claims.quote: Among people with normal G6PD levels taking primaquine, the most common adverse event is gastrointestinal upset, which can be minimized or eliminated if it is taken with food.

claims.text: Primaquine terminal chemoprophylaxis after prolonged exposure
claims.quote: terminal chemoprophylaxis for travelers who have had prolonged exposure to P. vivax or P. ovale in malaria-endemic areas

claims.text: G6PD hemolysis and quantitative test before primaquine
claims.quote: Primaquine can cause potentially life-threatening hemolysis in people with glucose-6-phosphate-dehydrogenase (G6PD) deficiency. G6PD deficiency must be ruled out with a quantitative laboratory test before prescribing primaquine to patients.

claims.text: Tafenoquine 200 mg loading daily for 3 days, weekly, 1 dose after; not for children; pregnancy/breastfeeding
claims.quote: Begin taking 3 days before travel to malaria-endemic areas with a loading dose of 200 mg daily for 3 days

claims.text: Tafenoquine one dose after leaving
claims.quote: Take 1 additional 200 mg dose in the week after leaving endemic areas

claims.text: Tafenoquine not for children
claims.quote: Not indicated for use in children

claims.text: Tafenoquine last-minute
claims.quote: Good for last-minute travelers because the drug is started 3 days before travel

claims.text: Tafenoquine breastfeeding needs infant G6PD
claims.quote: Contraindicated during pregnancy and breastfeeding unless the breastfed infant has a documented normal G6PD level

claims.text: Tafenoquine G6PD contraindication
claims.quote: Contraindicated in people with G6PD deficiency

claims.text: Not 100% effective; seek care for fever, get tested
claims.quote: Malaria chemoprophylaxis, while highly effective, is not 100% effective. Travelers should be advised to seek medical care immediately if fever develops, report their travel history, get tested for malaria

claims.text: Risk varies by adherence; suboptimal regimens raise risk
claims.quote: Risk also varies by travelers' adherence to mosquito precautions and chemoprophylaxis recommendations.

claims.text: Suboptimal regimen raises risk
claims.quote: Travelers who decline to take chemoprophylaxis, who receive a suboptimal drug regimen

claims.text: Symptoms from 7 days to several months or more
claims.quote: Malaria symptoms can develop as early as 7 days after being bitten by an infectious mosquito and as late as several months or more after exposure.

claims.text: Suspected malaria is a medical emergency; rapid deterioration
claims.quote: is a medical emergency requiring urgent intervention because clinical deterioration, including death, can occur rapidly and unpredictably.

claims.text: Severe disease features: kidney injury, ARDS, confusion, seizures, coma, death
claims.quote: In severe disease, acute kidney injury, acute respiratory distress syndrome, mental confusion, severe anemia, seizures, coma, and death can occur.

claims.text: Sick while traveling: seek care and continue prophylaxis until diagnosis
claims.quote: should seek the best available medical services as soon as possible, even if still traveling, and should continue their chemoprophylaxis regimen until they have a definitive diagnosis.

claims.text: Evaluate in facility with rapid diagnosis; results within hours
claims.quote: Patients suspected of having malaria should be urgently evaluated in a facility that is able to provide rapid diagnosis and treatment. Test results must be performed with results available immediately (within a few hours).

claims.text: Generally well tolerated; minor side effects
claims.quote: The drugs used for malarial chemoprophylaxis are generally well-tolerated. Minor side effects usually do not require stopping the drug.

claims.text: Missed dose: do not double
claims.quote: take the next dose with food as soon as possible; do not double the dose the day after the missed dose

claims.text: Weekly drug 1-2 days late: resume original day
claims.quote: If this is the case, the traveler can take a dose as soon as possible, then resume weekly doses on the originally scheduled day.

claims.text: Weekly drug more than 2 days late: new day
claims.quote: If the traveler is >2 days late, blood levels might not be adequate. The traveler should take a dose as soon as possible. The weekly doses should resume at this new day of the week

claims.text: Daily drug late: resume at new time
claims.quote: The traveler should take a dose as soon as possible and resume the daily schedule at the new time of day.

claims.text: Weekly drugs wider margin of error
claims.quote: drugs with longer half-lives, which are taken weekly, offer the advantage of a wider margin of error if the traveler is late with a dose.

claims.text: Overdose, especially chloroquine, fatal; childproof containers
claims.quote: Overdose of antimalarial drugs, particularly chloroquine, can be fatal and is a medical emergency. Medications should be stored in childproof containers out of reach of infants and children.

claims.text: Switching daily to weekly not recommended
claims.quote: Switching from a daily to a weekly chemoprophylaxis medication is not recommended because it takes time for the weekly medication to reach protective levels.

claims.text: Pregnancy: avoid travel optimal; malaria more severe
claims.quote: Because no chemoprophylaxis regimen is completely effective, avoidance of travel to areas with malaria transmission during pregnancy is optimal.

claims.text: Malaria more severe in pregnancy
claims.quote: Malaria infection can be more severe in pregnant than in nonpregnant women.

claims.text: Pregnancy: mefloquine only option in chloroquine-resistant areas
claims.quote: For travel to areas with chloroquine-resistant Plasmodium, mefloquine is the only medication recommended for malaria chemoprophylaxis during pregnancy.

claims.text: Pregnancy: chloroquine where no resistance
claims.quote: Pregnant women traveling to areas where chloroquine-resistant P. falciparum has not been reported can take chloroquine chemoprophylaxis.

claims.text: Pregnancy: A-P not recommended, doxy contraindicated, no primaquine/tafenoquine
claims.quote: Atovaquone-proguanil is not recommended for use during pregnancy because of limited availability of data on its safety and because other options are available.

claims.text: Pregnancy: doxycycline contraindicated
claims.quote: Doxycycline is contraindicated for malaria chemoprophylaxis during pregnancy

claims.text: Pregnancy: no primaquine or tafenoquine
claims.quote: Neither primaquine nor tafenoquine should be used during pregnancy

claims.text: Breast milk drug levels too low to protect infant
claims.quote: Antimalarial drug concentrations in breast milk are too low to protect nursing infants from malaria.

claims.text: Breastfeeding: A-P not for infants under 5 kg
claims.quote: Atovaquone-proguanil chemoprophylaxis is not recommended for lactating women when their infants weigh <5 kg (<11 lb) because of lack of safety data.

claims.text: Discourage buying abroad: counterfeit, substandard, contaminated
claims.quote: Travelers should be discouraged from obtaining chemoprophylaxis medications while abroad. Malaria chemoprophylaxis medications might be available at overseas destinations, including drugs not recommended in the United States; however, the quality of these products is often not known.

claims.text: Products might be counterfeit, substandard, contaminated
claims.quote: Products might be produced under substandard manufacturing practices, be counterfeit, contain contaminants

claims.text: Long-term travelers buy enough before leaving the US
claims.quote: strongly advise that before leaving the United States they purchase enough medication to last them for the entire duration of their travel to malaria-endemic areas.

claims.text: Malaria transmission mainly dusk to dawn
claims.quote: Malaria transmission occurs primarily between dusk and dawn because of the nocturnal feeding habits of Anopheles mosquitoes.

claims.text: Sunscreen first, repellent second
claims.quote: they should apply sunscreen first and insect repellent second.

claims.text: Review the exact itinerary
claims.quote: review the exact itinerary to determine if travel will occur in highly endemic areas.

claims.text: Consider detailed itinerary, accommodations, season, travel style, pregnancy
claims.quote: consider not only the destination but also the detailed itinerary, including specific cities, types of accommodations, season, and style of travel, as well as special health conditions (e.g., pregnancy).

claims.text: Drug choice factors: itinerary, resistance, adverse reactions, history, cost
claims.quote: When deciding which drug to use, consider the itinerary and length of trip, malaria drug resistance in the destination country, previous adverse reactions to antimalarials, drug allergies, medical history, and drug costs

claims.quote: Recommended drugs for each country are listed in alphabetical order and have comparable efficacy in that country.

claims.text: Doxycycline tends to be the least expensive
claims.quote: Tends to be the least expensive antimalarial

claims.text: Tafenoquine not recommended with psychotic disorders
claims.quote: Not recommended in those with psychotic disorders

claims.text: Primaquine breastfeeding needs infant G6PD test
claims.quote: Cannot be used by women who are breastfeeding unless the infant has also been tested for G6PD deficiency

claims.text: G6PD test only once; costs and delays
claims.quote: There are costs and delays associated with getting a G6PD test done; however, it only has to be done once. Once a normal G6PD level is verified and documented, the test does not have to be repeated

claims.text: About 2,000 cases; no malaria vaccine available in the US
claims.quote: There is no vaccine for malaria currently available in the U.S.

claims.text: Avoid bites even when taking medication
claims.quote: Avoid mosquito bites even if you are taking medications to prevent malaria.

claims.text: Acquired immunity weakens over time away
claims.quote: acquired immunity to (protection from) malaria weakens the longer you are away from an area where malaria is widespread or endemic.

claims.text: Get antimalarials in the US before travel
claims.quote: Get all your medications, including antimalarial drugs, in the US, before traveling overseas.

claims.text: Counterfeit or substandard drugs abroad
claims.quote: Be aware of counterfeit (fake) or substandard (not made according to U.S. standards) drugs sold in some countries.

claims.text: Discuss detailed itinerary, activities, accommodations, medical history with a provider
claims.quote: You should discuss with a healthcare provider a detailed itinerary of where you are traveling, your activities, accommodations, and your medical history

claims.text: Repellent active ingredients; DEET best
claims.quote: DEET (Insect repellents that contain DEET offer the best protection against mosquito bites.)

claims.text: Repellent list
claims.quote: Picaridin (known as KBR 3023 and icaridin outside the US) - IR3535 - Oil of lemon eucalyptus (OLE) - Para-menthane-diol (PMD) - 2-undecanon

claims.text: Clothing and permethrin; not on skin
claims.quote: Use 0.5% permethrin spray to treat clothing and gear (such as boots, pants, socks, and tents) or buy permethrin-treated clothing and gear. - Do not use permethrin products directly on skin.

claims.text: Loose long sleeves, pants and socks
claims.quote: Wear loose-fitting, long-sleeved shirts and pants and socks.

claims.text: Sleep in screened or air-conditioned room or under net
claims.quote: Sleep in a well-screened or air-conditioned room, or sleep under a permethrin-treated bed net.

claims.text: EPA-registered repellents
claims.quote: Use Environmental Protection Agency (EPA)-registered insect repellents with one of the active ingredients

claims.text: None protects 100%; fever up to one year needs care
claims.quote: Although malaria prevention strategies can be very effective, none will protect 100% of the time.

claims.text: Fever or flu-like illness up to one year: seek immediate care, tell travel history
claims.quote: If you have a fever or flu-like illness either while traveling in an area where malaria spreads or after returning home (for up to one year) seek immediate medical attention. Tell your healthcare provider about your travel history.

claims.text: Untreated: kidney failure, seizures, confusion, coma, death
claims.quote: If not treated right away, the infection can become serious. It may cause kidney failure, seizures, mental confusion, coma, and death.
